British Columbia-harbours and rivers-Old Massett-wharf repairs, $3,800.

I wish to supplement what
I was saying last night regarding the Public Works department in British Columbia. As a preface to what I have to say I would like to read an article from the Ottawa Citizen of last evening:
If both political parties had political wisdom, they would, in my judgment, come to an agreement by some binding pledge, to put an end forever to patronage, and free themselves as members from all worry and annoyance at the hands of place hunters. Candidates could then stand on their personal merits, on the merits of their party, their interest in their constituencies, in the welfare of the country at large, and the people would vote for them honestly on those considerations only. We would not then witness the painful exhibitions that I have seen of defeated candidates boasting that, though defeated, the patronage is still in their hands, because their party had won the election.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to get this article before the committee. I fail to understand why it is that representatives of constituencies 'have placed upon them the duty of going through the country investigating requests made by the people in the matter of public works. They are put to great expense and have to travel very often in the most inclement weather, as it is frequently during the winter months that the members must travel. They travel through the country and go to great pains to get the facts to present to parliament, and then they come here only to discover that anything they aay has no possible chance of having any attention paid to it, for the simple reason that they are not members or supporters of the government in power.
Last December I visited the northern section of British Columbia, putting in three weeks there under great hardship and incurring considerable expense. I went there to find out just what the people needed, and to satisfy myself that I was working in accord with the government engineer, I took a trip to Victoria, six hundred miles away, and presented to him what the people had given to me. I told him that I did not wish to advocate anything which he did not consider was right and proper. I hold in my hand a letter from the federal engineer, in which he says that the various public works

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
that I asked for .receive his absolute support. He has the following to say in the last paragraph :
If there are any other items which you consider it necessary to include in these estimates I shall be pleased to have a list of them at your convenience.
But what do I find? I find, Mr. Chairman and members of this committee, that after going to every possible care and trouble, and presenting to the Minister of Public Works these requests for the northern and central parts of British Columbia, when the estimates are brought down there is only one item for wharf repairs at Old Massett. The federal engineer's report on necessary public works showed an expenditure of $79,365, not counting $30,000 for river improvements and snag boat operations on some of the rivers there. But what do I find? I find that in this constituency of Skeena, which has an immense Pacific seaooast and where is carried on the largest fishing industry in the whole of Canada, their great need for. wharves and roads has been entirely overlooked.
The people of Canada are asking the same question that I am going to ask. Is it right that the most important department in the whole of the government's activities, the Department of Public Works, should be placed under political patronage? Is it possible, because a member happens to come from a constituency once Liberal or Conservative, that the people are to be penalized for that? Surely the Department of Public Works should be outside the realm of politics altogether. If the government realize the importance of building up our young country, I cannot see why they should not take the steps that are necessary.
In reading the report of the Ontario Department of Health for 1928 I find that out of 57,521 official certificates issued last year, 61 per cent were issued for emigration purposes. That means that 34,000 young Canadians left this province to go into the United States. In British Columbia we are faced with great problems. We have the orient right at our door; we find that a seepage is steadily going on there, and the government is doing very little to hold our own people in the country.
A wharf costing only four or five hundred , dollars is denied because the government, to my mind, seemingly lack vision, when they think that intelligent people will be won over and brought to their knees in submission to any party in power who refuse to give them what they are entitled to.
Why should a member of parliament be obligated to come here asking for these things,
when there is a federal engineer appointed by the government to send in reports on necessary public works? We are absolutely like children when we come to the major elements of government. Why should a member of parliament, I say again, have to come here and beg, as if it were a personal favour, for what is of national importance? Surely a government which, by being placed in power, has received the highest gift which a nation can bestow upon it, should be over and above party interests and look for the good of the country from east to west.
Hear, hear.

I hear an hon. gentleman
from the old province of Quebec saying, "hear, hear." I am proud to have that "hear, hear;" but I would be much prouder and happier if I thought the province of Quebec joined with me in my supplication that the public works department be taken outside of political patronage.
It is.

It is not, I am sorry. I
do not want to go into personalities, but when the Deputy Minister of Public Works was passing through British Columbia last year, when he came into the town of Prince Rupert -and I was there-to whom did he go? Did he come and ask the representative to consult with him? No, he went to those that I know are not working as they ought to work over and above party interests. I have never yet accused and I shall never accuse a man unless I am on sound principles, but I know that many necessary public works which are for the building up of that young province, which are works supported by Liberals and Conservatives, or, in other words, by the people, have to be recommended by one who no longer sits in this parliamentary assembly. We are handing down a legacy of hate instead of a legacy of peace and of hope. As long as we continue in the mood we are in to-day where we are passing every paltry little public work as a bouquet for the member to go back and say to his constituents: "See what I got for you," we are doing groat injury to the future of Canada. Is there any intelligent man who to-day thinks that this is going to continue? It will not. The hour must come when we shall have to change our ways and take out of the realm of politics what is for the nation's good.
Last winter at the request of three or four people I went sixty miles away over the waters in order that I might discover their needs. I went into a storm, the worst that had struck the Pacific coast for years. I was out on the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
water storm-tossed for two days and nights, never knowing whether the boat would reach land or not. Our boat was swept by the stormy seas; we were there baling out tons of water at midnight. What for? Hon. members may say: you are only posing. I would not be in the house to-day if I were posing. When I arrived at my destination I found a family that had been without supplies for days. I found them, mother and children, cut off from every chance of getting in touch with any of their fellowmen and this at ihe festive season of Christmas.
The day is coming when throughout the length and breadth of Canada truth will prevail. It will come in spite of every material force that ever man put into execution. It is coming because the heart of the people is true and they know the truth when they hear it. No longer can members of the government go through the length and breadth of Canada and tell the people about the misdeeds of their opponents. Why should we talk about what the other party did? Let us get rid of the defects of the past and let us stand upon a common platform. Surely the Liberal party, represented by hon. gentlemen opposite, and the Conservative party, represented by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house, have major platforms, big principles upon which they can go to the country, and we should leave out the trivial things that we hear so much about.
I want to ask the government and particularly the Minister of Public Works this question. I have brought forward not one but several public works that I believe are necessary. Do they honestly believe that those public works which I have presented this year are required? British Columbia will one day be the prid'e of Canada' because her wealth in natural resources is beyond the dreams of human possibility. Do they believe that because British Columbia is separated from the rest of Canada by the great Rocky mountains, it is not to be considered when public works and public development are under consideration? Surely British Columbia, which is now coming forward so strongly and capably, is entitled to consideration. A father is bound to look to the interests of his children; a city is bound to see to the health and welfare of its citizens, and I say that the federal government, which has taken upon its shoulders the Public Works department, should do what is essential. I cannot prove it, but I feel sure that there are in these estimates that we are now passing millions of dollars that it is not essential to expend, and this money should be spent throughout Canada where public works 
are absolutely essential. You know it, Mr. Chairman, and I know it. What is going to be the end of all this? The end is very evident. The people of Canada to-day are becoming educated to this extent, that they recognize merit and truth, and can separate it from falsehood and hypocrisy, and until the government treats this matter of public works differently, and takes each province and each constituency on its merits, regardless of how it may have voted, and gets the federal engineers to give an honest report as to the public works that are essential, we are only blinding ourselves and are guilty of folly. I come to this House of Commons with a motive which I think no man can challenge There is no man who can challenge my love of the people and my regard for their welfare. We all probably feel that way, but I can say this, that I can go back to my constituency feeling assured that I have done my duty faithfully to the people, even though the government may turn deaf ears to my presentations and . the needs of the people who are entitled to be heard.
How can the government answer this question? Why did they remove from the estimates the appropriation put in for a float for the fishermen at Prince Rupert? Why was that taken out of the estimates? First, why was it put in? We see there a dilemma. If the floats were necessary in the first place, they are doubly and trebly necessary now. The port of Prince Rupert is the largest fishing port on the North American continent, and hon. gentlemen know it. We find that of the output of salmon and halibut for the whole of Canada, the port of Prince Rupert exports over sixty per cent. Now I want to know why the government took out of the estimates that appropriation, especially when to-day the fishing fleet at Prince Rupert has increased three-fold. I have photographs here, showing the greatest congestion at that port. I ask again, why was that appropriation taken out of the estimates?
Some of the eastern members have but a vague idea of the port of Prince Rupert. It is unfortunately true that the people of the east cannot travel as much as they should to the west, but that port, I can tell hon. gen. tlemen, is growing rapidly, and despite the treatment which it is getting at the hands of this government to-day I have faith enough to believe that the port of Prince Rupert will become a leading Pacific port. The people of British Columbia are a people brought up among the great mountains that rear their tops to heaven, and if you study the history of the world, you will find that

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
the mountaineers have always been the great leaders in every forward move of civilization. So I would say to the government now, please forget this little thing of trying to get even. Just forget it and rise to the height to which you ought to rise, namely, to a broad vision of the welfare of the whole people, and where it is necessary that money be expended on public works, let the expenditures be made for the good of the country at large, regardless of whether the constituency is represented by a Progressive, a Conservative or a Liberal.

I have listened with close attention to the strong plea made by my hon. friend from Skeena. I differ from him, however, because I do not believe that the estimates are drafted in such a partisan way as he complains of, because otherwise there would have been no item of 8500,000 for Toronto, which is ' not represented in this house by any Liberal member. There are also other items in the estimates for counties which are represented by members of the opposition in this house. I understood my hon. friend from Skeena to say that the appropriations in the estimates are presented to members on the government side as if they were bouquets for them to present to their electors after the close of the session. Is the hon. member complaining of that?

I do not complain about
money being expended where it is necessary, but the money should be expended because the work in question is a work of merit, and no member should look upon an appropriation as a bouquet handed over to him. But many of them do, because I have heard them say, and I have no doubt the hon. gentleman will agree with me, "I got this for you, and I got that for you." Is that true or not?

My hon. friend is asking
for a bouquet for himself perhaps.
No, sir, no bouquet for me.

If the hon. member
for Temiscouata is answering for the Minister of Public Works, will he tell the committee why the item that was in the estimates Inst year for the fishermen's float at Prince Rupert has been taken out of the estimates?

But my hon. friend from
Skeena spoke of so many things that I forgot his main point.
I should like to get squarely from the minister why this item was taken out of the estimates.

I do not imagine the item has been in the estimates while I have been
in charge of the department.
Yes, it was.

If so, I would not have
heard complaints about nothing being in the estimates for Skeena, complaints that are made every session when the British Columbia votes are under consideration. I take it that this must have been some time ago.
No, sir.

According to the reports
received by the department, there is a difference of opinion among the fishermen as to what is the proper location for the float at Skeena. Probably that is the main reason why further progress has not been made in this connection. I am surprised at my hon. friend, who I know is very serious and would not for the world misrepresent any hon, gentleman, particularly members of the government-I am surprised, I say, at his asking if the government do believe in British Columbia and that western section of Canada. Certainly every member of the government entertains that belief, and they feel that they have done fairly well by that section of the Dominion. He will find that of the $539,000 for British Columbia, not one dollar is being spent in a Liberal riding.
It is hard to find any Liberal members from British Columbia.

According to my hon.
friend's argument, if there were no Liberal members from British Columbia the province would get nothing. I think my hon. friend realizes that British Columbia has fared very well. His suggestion as to political patronage entering into these estimates has, I think, been conclusively answered by my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). There are supplementary estimates coming, but I am not in a position to say whether the ridings that are not represented by government supporters will fare better in those supplementaries than they have in the main estimates. Up to the present, however, the government has done very well for my hon. friend's riding and the other ridings in British Columbia, and it intends to continue to treat the province fairly in spite of the criticisms of my hon. friend.

The appropriation of $15,-
000 appeared in the main estimates for 1925. The appropriation for the Stewart wharf was likewise included. Both were taken out. The minister's answer to me is similar to that which he has given to other members, but it is not convincing. It would be far from me

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
to say that as a general rule the Public Works department does not stretch out to embrace all the provinces, but the-fact remains that these absolutely essential appropriations were discontinued. The minister tells me that the reports he received disclose a difference of opinion amongst the fishermen regarding the location of the float. I ask the minister for the source of his information and for the names of the parties.

That is the report received from the district engineer. I may tell my hon. friend that the proportion of the present votes for British Columbia to the total estimates compares very favourably with the figures of other years. In my opinion this fact alone fully answers my hon. friend's criticism.

I want to get this matter
cleared up, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Public Works says that he has done more for British Columbia than what was done in past years. That may be so. But this does not explain why the appropriation was withdrawn, for to say that his action was based on a report that a few of the fishermen were in doubt about the location of the float is by no means an adequate explanation. The fishing industry is very important to Canada, and should be encouraged. The minister placed the onus on the federal engineer in Victoria. I know a little about the sources of information, I wish the committee to consider this: I am the representative of the people of my riding, Liberal and Conservative, labour and commercial, and they have come to me and requested that the appropriation should be reinstated in the estimates. Do you,_ sir, or does any other member of the committee think that I, who for years taught the sons and daughters of these people, would degrade myself by putting forward something that I had not thoroughly examined? Yet my judgment and my integrity are apparently of no account to the Minister of Public Works or his department in comparison with the other sources of information to which he refers. Surely this is not in accord with the principles of democratic government. Then take another matter, the post office in Prince Rupert. The accommodation is a farce. The people of the city were opposed to renewing the lease of the premises, and yet their views were disregarded. Why? As to the float, the fishermen have requested that it be built, and all the business people of the city, including the board of trade-and they are mostly Liberals-have supported that request. Yet nothing is done. There may be an appropriation for the work in the supplement-aries; I know not; but I do contend that it is

of vital import to the people who are building up this country and adding to its revenue that they should be given proper accommodation, and I cannot see any reason why this float should not be built. Does the minister think that I am speaking merely for the pleasure of doing so? I went to Victoria, travelling 600 miles odd, to interview the federal engineer. I went at my own expense and in my own time so that I might get the engineer to give me an idea of the situation in order that I might come to Ottawa feeling that at least I had gone to the trouble of presenting things rightly. And what did he tell me? The federal engineer told me exactly what I have stated to the minister, namely, that certain works were necessary. I have a list of these works. First, there is Bella Coola: for wharf repairs $6,700 is required. Then Digby island, repairs to approach, $2,600; Hartley bay, wharf, $4,600; New Massett, wharf repairs, $2,050; Old Massett-that is the one that appears in the estimates here; Port Clements, $715; Prince Rupert floats, $16,000; Queen Charlotte city, proposed wharf repairs, $4,000; Queen Charlotte city, proposed repairs, $1,900; and Stewart, extension to the proposed wharf $38,000.
In addition to these I gave to the minister a list of other necessary public works that involved my going hundreds of miles-

Can my hon. friend give
us any information as to the location-
Yes, I shall tell you.

-on which the people
would be agreed?

The people are agreed that the north end of the present drydock is a perfect natural location, easily within reach of the city and sufficiently sheltered to enable a wharf to be put up there. But they object to Seal cove. I went there myself and I know something about the place. There is no road and on dark nights it would be dangerous to pass through the channel to the proposed site. The fishermen object to going so far away from the city.
I do not wish to elaborate this, but I would point out to the minister that I went to Victoria for the purpose of getting from the federal engineer a plan of the proposed work to be built at Seal cove. I agree with the minister that there was a doubt as to which site was preferable. Cow bay or Seal cove, but that was a matter that could have been easily adjusted. The point was that the floats were needed. So long as it was understood by the federal government and the provincial and

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
municipal authorities that the work was needed, the site was not at all a question to worry about.
I put in some further estimates: Float at Metlakahtla, an Indian fishing village, where there is no float at all. Last year, two Indians were reported drowned going to get their boat, a storm having arisen. That would cost $1,200. Clearing Whitesail and Ootsa rivers: all that is needed here is $2,000; for removal of five little log jams, that are there and give portage of 238 miles of the finest lake water that Canada possesses. All round these lakes there are farmers, and people are going in to build up the country. Next on the list are floats for Francois lake. If hon. members here realized what a heritage British Columbia is, what a wonderful country is there, what it is going to be, and the increasing numbers of people who are going into that country, they would be astonished; even the people of old Ontario who live by the mighty St. Lawrence would open their eyes in wonder. It is indeed a wonderful country-wonderful in the extent of its fertility, its beauty, and its splendid water transportation. We ask for five little floats, not costing S100 each, to be placed along the Francois lake, so that farmers may come from Nadina which is sixty miles away. Those farmers are obliged to transport their produce sixty miles along a poor road, whereas all they would have to do would be to go down to the water's edge to a little wharf and go sixty miles upstream at no small cost. Then there is needed a float at Allison harbour, as well as repairs to the wharf at Silver City, Alice Arm; a breakwater at Oona river and a warehouse and wharf at Aiyansh.

It is not my intention to criticize this item particularly, but I should like the minister to give a brief explanation. In putting that question to him I will take the opportunity of bringing to the attention of the committee the Public Works Act which wias under discussion last night, because under this item will arise an opportunity, if such were contemplated or desired, of abusing the privileges Which is accorded to the minister under this act. I am speaking now in a very general sense and I am not in any way suggesting that such is the intention of the present minister. I want to point out the danger of a rather loose interpretation of the act. The total vote for dredging is $1,715,000, and it gives into the hands of the minister a very large sum of money to be used generally throughout the different provinces of Canada. Section 36 of part II of the Public Works Act, chapter 166 of the revised statutes, volume 3, is the section which controls not only this minister but other ministers in the expenditure of money. I will read the section and then I wish to make one or two brief comments. Section 36 reads:
Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of any department of the government, the minister having charge of such department shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest; or
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department; or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than five thousand dollars and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
I fear that the minister's interpretation o-f paragraph (b) of this section is that he is at liberty, whenever he feels' like it, to do any work of any value under the direct control of the department by day labour and not by tender. I do not concede that to be the intention of the act. Obviously the intention of the act is that the department doing work shall invite tenders by public advertisement. Then it makes these three exceptions. One refers to an emergency such as war, fire or

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
something else that requires immediate work to be done. Paragraph (b) is the controversial one. It reads:
In which from the nature of the -work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
In other words the act says that if it can in certain circumstances be deadly demonstrated by engineers' findings and incontrovertible evidence that the work can be done more expeditiously and economically by the officers and servants of the department, the minister is released of the (Obligation of calling for tenders. It never was contemplated that under the section the minister should have the discretionary power of saying whether the work should be done by tender or otherwise. In other words the act imposes upon the minister an obligation always to' call for tenders unless certain very specific reasons can be adduced to the contrary. To digress for a minute, I think the minister said last night that it was the policy of the government to follow certain lines. If it is the minister's intention to take advantage of paragraph (b) to do certain works, no matter what the cost is, by day labour, then the act ought to be changed. Either the act ought to be changed to make it clear that its intent is as I read and understand it, or the section should be modified so as to make it perfectly clear that the minister has the discretion whether he calls for tenders or not.
This is not a new controversy in the house. Long before the minister came into the house the question was discussed time and time again; but never before did I know a minister to take a stand other than the one that I took last night, namely, that where the w-ork was to cost less than $5,000 it was optional with the minister whether he should call for tenders or not. That was always claimed, I think extravagantly anid unreasonably claimed by ministers in the past, but I never before heard a minister assert that paragraph (b) gave him a sort of discretionary power. Even paragraph (c) shows that it is incumbent upon the minister to determine whether, by the nature of the work-that is, where it is to cost under $5,000-it is advisable not to call for tenders. He must even then be certain that it is better to do the work without tender. In other words the section is this, that wherever it is possible to do the work by tender, it must be done by tender. The duty is then imposed upon the minister to be prepared to show parliament that where tenders were not called for he could get the work done better, cheaper, more' economically, more expeditiously, without calling for
tenders. I wish to associate section 36 with the interpretation that I have given of it. I put that forward as my view in connection wdth the expenditure of this very large sum of $1,715,000 for dredging. My submission is that in the expenditure of this sum, as in other cases, it is obligatory for the minister to call for tenders except where he can Show clearly that the work can be done more expeditiously otherwise.

I quite agree with that.

Therefore the question of letting the work by day labour or contract will enter into a small proportion. I have read the act with some care myself and I think that is the interpretation of it. But the practice not merely under this government but for years has been to do the works which, first of all, the local engineer recommends can be better done by day labour. Sometimes, of course, the chief engineer disagrees with him and says, No, you had better do the work by contract. Then the matter comes to the deputy minister, and then to the minister in charge. There are cases where it is more convenient to do the work by day labour. I want to say very frankly that the duties of the minister are much lighter when it is done by contract. I do not want to say positively, but my information is that the Department of Justice some years ago gave a ruling on the subject which is in accordance with the practice that has been followed for twenty years at any rate.

International bridge over St. Croix river between St. Croix, N.B., and Vanceboro, Maine, the state of Maine to contribute the sum of $2,000, $4,000.

This revote of $4,000 is required for the completion of the international bridge over the St. Croix river, under contract with C. A. Noyes of Orono, Maine, at a contract price of $14,797.65. 'Mr. GARDINER: This is an international waterway?
Yes.

The province is not in it at all; this is an agreement between the federal government and the state of Maine.

Are there no international complications?
No.

Is this agreement between the federal government and the state of Maine or between the federal government and the United States?
Mr. ELLIOTT': It is between the federal government and the state of Maine.

The system in the United States is different from our system; the state has a larger jurisdiction than our province. The state contributes its portion to an international arrangement of this kind, to which the federal government is a party.

speechtext:

speechtext: What is the amount?

better advised to wait until he knows what parts of those lines have been sold and what is required for the maintenance of the lines which the government still own and operate. I do not think a motion of that kind would be advisable at present coming from the minister or anyone else.

Miscellaneous-National Gallery of Canada, $135,000.
What is the reason for the increase?
The trustees have requested an additional $35,000, and they have been given that larger appropriation.

What explanation ha*
been made to justify the demand for more money?

This amount is required to provide for operation and maintenance, workshop supplies, upkeep of premises, purchase of works of art. The addition over last year is to enable the board to complete the purchase of some pictures which they have in mind to purchase.
About how much is expended yearly?

The full vote is spent every year.
Supply-Public Works
Does the department calculate on a certain appropriation for the national gallery every year?
Yes.
About how much?
Usually $100,000.

I have been asked to make a protest in regard to the closing hours of the national gallery. In the first place I should like to ask the minister whether the hours of closing of the national gallery are regulated by early closing in the city of Ottawa; is it correct that the gallery closes at four o'clock in the afternoon, daylight time, or three o'clock standard time?
My information is that it follows the same time that we follow in the house, that is daylight saving time.

That is exactly the point of protest. The people of the rest of the Dominion of Canada go on standard time. Last year there came to this city a representative from my district who is very much interested in art and after his business was concluded he had just one hour to spare for a visit to the art gallery. Under all ordinary conditions he would have been able to visit the gallery for that one hour, but on account of the early closing he failed to have that opportunity. That man will probably not have an opportunity in the next ten years of making a similar visit and I was asked on his behalf to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. Why should the people of the whole Dominion of Canada be inconvenienced to the extent of that one hour to give the people of the city of Ottawa an hour of extra daylight? The position taken by the gentleman appealed to me as being very fair and reasonable. If this property is being operated for the people of the whole of Canada, it is quite reasonable that they should expect it to be open the same hours as if it were run on standard time which prevails throughout Canada.

That is just one of the things that apparently happen in every place that is being run on daylight saving time, a time different from that in use in other places. But may I call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that if the visitor had come from Montreal, Toronto, or any other place having daylight saving time, he would not have noticed the difference. It is the rural sections that are perhaps prejudiced.

The same thing would apply to a man who wanted to hear the debates in the house. He might be fortunate if he found himself an hour late.
That would depend upon what estimates were under consideration?
Probably so. He would not fare quite as badly if estimates were under consideration as if some matters were before the house.
That might be true too.

The matter is worth considering, and I thank my hon. friend for bringing it to the attention of the committee. I do not know that I can make any promise that there will be much in the way of results, but I shall be glad to look into the matter.

Four o'clock is an early
hour for the gallery to close. It could surely remain open as long as the museum.

Suppose it opened an
hour earlier in the morning?

Is the museum open
on Saturday afternoon?

Yes, and on Sunday. I
think my hon. friend is wrong , about the hour of four o'clock; I think it is five o'clock, daylight saving.

Four o'clock was certainly
the hour that was given to me. This gentleman had business in various departments, and after that was done, he said that it was three o'clock by his time, standard time. He went to an attendant in the House of Commons to be directed to the museum, but was told there was no use going there at that hour as the museum closed at four o'clock.

The reason I asked
the question was that a lady and gentleman came here on Saturday afternoon and found the museum closed. They were told it closed every Saturday afternoon.
Mr. McQUARRjIE:	It is not everyone,
unfortunately, who can come to Ottawa to see the pictures in the national gallery, and I think that the policy which has been adopted by the directors of loaning some of the pictures to other centres to be placed on exhibition is highly to be commended. I know that in New Westminster, through the kindness of the directors, we have for several years been receiving from the national gallery very fine exhibits of pictures, which have been viewed by many thousands of people, and I think that that kind of thing should be

Supply-Public Works
encouraged. There is some charge in connection with the sending out of these pictures, transportation and insurance charges, and so forth, but it is not generally known that the pictures in the gallery are available for that purpose, and I think it would be well if that fact were more generally known, because ordinarily these wonderful pictures in the gallery. cannot be seen unless one comes to Ottawa.

I do not
just get the point raised by the minister. He said that there would be no special inconvenience to people coming here from say Montreal or Toronto, where they have daylight saving time. I would remind him that no matter whether they have standard or daylight saving time in these places, they come to Ottawa on trains running on standard time. It is very commendable that there should be a gallery of this kind, and the name "National" indicates that it is for the whole nation, and not solely for the benefit of the citizens of Ottawa. It is a fact that while many cities and towns, including Ottawa, have adopted daylight saving, the great mass of the people in the country districts, are still on God's time, standard time. You are spending another '$35,000 to get some extra fine pictures for the gallery, for whose benefit? Obviously people from outside points will not have the same opportunity that the citizens of Ottawa will have to see these pictures, because of the early closing of the gallery. I think this is a matter in connection wth which the minister ought to get results. He says that he cannot promise anything definite- This is a case where he should promise something definite. He should be definite enough to say that the people outside Ottawa will have a reasonable opportunity to see these pictures and take advantage of the gallery, notwithstanding any difference in time there might be.

I have a good deal of
sympathy with what my hon. friend says, but I think he did not get my point when I said that while it did not make any difference to the people who came from Montreal or Toronto, 'which were on the same time as Ottawa, daylight saving time, it did make a difference to those who came in from the country, and that point deserves consideration.
What my hon. friend from New Westminster has said is very pertinent. I think that principle of loaning pictures should be extended as far as practicable. This gallery is the national gallery of Canada, and that
is the reason why in their wisdom those in charge have seen fit to allow the pictures to be loaned to different local galleries, so that the people there will have the opportunity of seeing them, which they would not have unless they paid a visit to the national gallery. I shall be glad to look into the matter and do the very best I can.

When I
referred to people coming in from the country, I did not mean people coming in from Carleton county or from anywhere in the immediate vicinity of Ottawa, who would walk in or come in on a bicycle. I presume that people from the rural districts many miles away from Ottawa would come in on the same trains as people coming from Toronto and Montreal, and they would be inconvenienced so far as Ottawa being on daylight saving time is concerned.

How much was spent
m buying pictures tlast year?
I have not that information here, but my hon. friend will find a list of the pictures bought in the report of the national gallery.

It is to be placed in the library, I understand.

more prominent place, for no man has reflected greater glory on this country in a literary way than Alpheus Todd.

I do not think there
is a more important bill, from the point of view of public affairs, and I will give my reasons in a few moments.
This company was incorporated in 1865, under 28 Victoria, chapter 43, as the Sun Insurance Company of Montreal. Under the charter it was given the right to carry on fire, marine, accident and guarantee insurance, and also life insurance. The powers granted were never used except in regard to life insurance, and very slightly in regard to accident insurance. The capitalization authorized was $2,000,000 in one hundred dollar shares, $800,000 to be subscribed and $100,000 to be paid up and invested. This capitalization covered the life branch.
In 1870 this act was amended by 33 Victoria, chapter 58, and the life insurance business was separated distinctly from the general business, The amendment of that year authorized a capital for the fife branch of $1,000,000, which might be increased to $2,000,000, solely for this branch. The same capitalization was permitted for the fire, marine and guarantee branch. Separate accounts of the expenses, profits and claims, losses, liabilities and assets were to be kept. The obvious intent of the charter at that time was to limit the capital of the company to $2,000,000 in respect of life, and $2,000,000 in respect of its general business.
In 1871 business was commenced, and the name was changed to The Sun Mutual Life Insurance Company of Montreal. The life and accident operations were united, and at that time everything inconsistent with these new provisions was repealed. In 1882 the name was again changed to the Sun Life Assurance Company and permission was granted to invest funds in foreign countries. In 1897 the investment powers were extended to include real estate in Canada and bonds and debentures of municipalities in the United States.
It will be noted in passing, Mr. Speaker, that shortly after the passing of this act the investment policy of the company was changed. Up to that time it had been doing a good deal of business in the way of mortgages, real estate loans, and so on, but suddenly the policy was switched and the policyholders' money was invested in the most speculative kind of industrial stocks, chiefly the traction stocks.
In 1871, when the business started, the capital subscribed was $500,000, 10 per cent of which was paid up, or $50,000 in cash. In 1876 another $12,000, or per cent, was paid up, making a total of $62,500. From 1876 to

and interests has not, however, enabled the company to pay these dividends, and from time to time the directors have resorted to various devices for the purpose of increasing the shareholders' account, so as to enable it to pay the dividends which have been paid.
The first of these devices was to credit the practically defunct accident branch with considerable sums of money, upon the theory that that branch in years past had been charged more than its proportion of the general expenses of the company. The accident branch being so credited out of the current profits, the sums so credited were brought into the shareholders' account for the purpose of augmenting it and so enabling the dividends to be paid. Three sums were so credited to the accident branch and brought in to the detriment of the policyholders and in the case of the shareholders; $2,000 in 1895; $4,000 in 1900; and $30,000 in 1902; and the evidence is that there are still at the credit of the accident branch considerable sums of money, the intention being to bring these also into the shareholders' account. It is manifest that in revising the charges made in past years to the accident branch, the directors of the present day have undertaken to overrule what may be presumed to have been the well-informed and deliberate decision of the directors of former years as to the proper proportion of expenses to be charged to that branch, and your commissioners think it clear that the revision was undertaken solely as a device for maintaining the shareholders' account.
Note again what your commissioners have said in this regard:
Another improper means by which the shareholders' account has been enabled to provide the dividends paid to shareholders is by similarly revising the rate of interest allowed upon capital in addition to its share of the profits in past years. The method adopted has been to go through the years as far back as 1877 and to allow, instead of the rates which were allowed, a rate of six per cent, which has been improved at six per cent, compound interest, from 1877 down. The result of this has been to bring into the shareholders' account $9,088.34 (in 1901).
A third method of swelling the shareholders' account has been to go back to the year 1897, when the new capital was issued at a premium of $30 per share-
That is the $2,000 to which I have just referred :
-and to bring into the general shareholders' account interest, compounded at six per cent, upon that premium. This revision of the earlier dealing with this premium, to the prejudice of policyholders, was also, in the opinion of your commissioners, improper. In this way the shareholders' account was swollen in 1905 by the sum of $37,930.73.
Is it any wonder that this company has been able to pay admirable dividends to its fortunate shareholders? But what of the policyholders? The commissioners continue:
Still a fourth method of maintaining the shareholders' account was to take out of moneys

Can the minister tell us what the average annual payment is to one of these rural carriers?

That is determined by distance and frequency of service. TheTe are rural routes in the Dominion which have a service only twice a week; there are others with three services, four services and six services weekly. Others are more frequent. And the mileage varies in all these routes; it is very seldom that we have two routes with about the same mileage. It would be impossible to give any average.

With regard to the rural mail carriers, particularly in Ontario and in the section from which I come, I can say very definitely that they are the poorest paid members of the civil service of this country. And they are the hardest worked; they work six days a week and almost every day in the year with the exception of four holidays. These men are not paid anything like the remuneration paid the city carriers. Moreover, they have to supply horse and rig, pay large expenses for upkeep of that equipment, and every day, in all conditions of weather, in all seasons of the year, very often on bad roads, they have to be on the job. Frequently it takes them almost the whole day to make the rounds of their route. Let me cite one specific instance which will typify all the rest. In one rural route the mail carrier covers fifteen miles every day and he receives S750 per annum, which amounts to about $2.40 per trip. He has only four holidays in the year.
Six.

He has to keep his horse and buggy, has to shoe the horse whenever necessary, and must meet all expenses in connection with his outfit. Hay at the present time costs almost $30 a ton and oats from seventy cents to a dofliliar per bushel. A budhel of oats will keep a horse about three days, and he requires from six to seven tons of hay a year. It costs $250 to shoe a horse, and if the carrier has to buy
new shoea that means between $5 and $6. Altogether, they estimate that the cost of shoeing a horse and keeping up a rig is about $70 a year. This man has to keep a family the same as the man in the city, although he gets very much less. The minimum wage for the city letter carrier is $1,080, with a maximum of $1,500, and he gets two suits per annum. He has no equipment whatever to keep up. So that the rural route men do not get enough for the work they do, notwithstanding that it is very much harder work than the city carriers perform.
The minister says the work is done by contract; we know it is. But there are circumstances in which the inspector does try to pare them down, and in order to keep their position they will reduce the price to less than cost of service. One reason why they do this is that many of these men have no money whatever. They have their horse and rig and if they lose their contract they can hardly sell that outfit. Many of these men have been in the service quite a number of years, and hardly know what else to do. I know one or two men who could not do anything else, so they will submit to having their tenders reduced in order to retain their positions.

I can say
definitely to the minister that they are reduced, and I know one man in my own town who was reduced almost half less than a year ago.

I thought my hon. friend had given the name.

No, they do not carry passengers, although they do carry parcels and manage to increase their income to some extent in that way. They some times carry bread into the country districts, and of course they carry some parcels. I have known of instances, although I cannot give the names, where inspectors have come out from the city and had each man tender against the other. The inspector would go to one man

and say, " Mr. So-and-So has tendered for so much; can you beat it?" Then he would go to the other man and say, " Can you beat this tender?" That Bort of thing has happened several times; these particular instances I mentioned happened some years ago. I know the minister does not know all about these matters; he is giving the facts as he knows them, but he is not on the job to see how these men work. Many times these mail carriers must wait for hours when a train is late; they are late getting out and late getting home, and unless some of them rent a little field where they grow oats and hay, they cannot carry on.

As I have quite a number of mail carriers in my constituency I should like to inform this committee of the satisfaction which they seem to have with the way they are treated by the department. A number of mail contracts were recently renewed in my constituency and I have not heard one of the contractors complain that he is not receiving sufficient remuneration for his services. I believe the tender principle is the most practical method which could be adopted by the department. As members of this committee know, these mail carriers cannot be given a great deal more than they are receiving because this rural mail service is maintained to encourage the rural people to remain on their farms, and it is maintained by the department at a great loss. If the contract prices seem to be low we must not forget that that is the fault of those who tender. Not long ago I had a new mail delivery established in my constituency in the St. Romain district, and I must congratulate the minister for giving us this delivery. the benefit of the country at large. So I believe it is rather unfair for hon. members of this house to try to introduce the idea that this system of calling for tenders should be changed; I think such a change would be prejudicial to the country at large.

May I draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that the opinion was expressed very freely on the floor of the house last winter that the Post Office depart-fnent should not be a surplus department; that is, that we should if possible endeavour to live within the revenue, but not look for large surpluses.
Balance your budget.

Yes. That is, we should
spend the revenue from the postal service in giving the people a better service. It will be noticed that when there is an increase in expenditure there is also an increase in revenue. I think it was in 1926 that we reduced the postage from three to two cents, and I think it will be found by looking carefully into the records that the house was then told that there would be a deficit of between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000 owing to that decrease in the postage rate, provided that the business did not increase. The business has increased to
such an extent in Canada in the last three years that that $6,000,000 has practically disappeared. The difference in revenue to-day as oompared with what it was in 1926. when the postage was three cents on letters and first-class mail matter is under $1,000,000.

The people are asking for it, the service is required, and the only regret I have, as the head of the department is that I cannot meet all the demands made on the department, many of which I know are honestly made for service that is really needed. I made a statement the other night, just to give an idea to the committee how I feel about giving service to the country in the proper distribution of the mails. I said that in the sparsely settled districts, in some cases isolated districts, where people receive but one mail a week, they might as well receive none, and that that kind of service should no longer be tolerated in Canada. I have attempted, and I am attempting in all cases of that kind, to give a better service. We have instances where our mailmen have travelled from twenty to twenty-five miles to get to isolated points where the revenue is only forty or fifty dollars a year, and yet to get there has cost the country the sum of $500 or $600 to give the service to these people.
